name: csv-zero (Zig SIMD CSV field iterator)
baseline: zsv (C library, built from src/c/zsv with 'cc -O3 main.c -lzsv'; labelled 'zsc (c)' in the result CSV) and lazycsv (C++ header library, g++ -O3 -march=native); Rust simd-csv and csv also measured
workload: Iterate a whole CSV file and count its fields with a 64 KB input buffer (csv-race harness): four real-world files (nfl.csv, worldcitiespop.csv, GTFS mbta stop-times, game.csv) and generated files from about 1 KB to about 9.9 GB, with and without quoting.
claimed_speedup: csv-race result-all.csv wall times, csv-zero vs zsv (C) vs lazycsv (C++): ~32 MB no-quotes 52 col 6.62 ms vs 14.1 ms vs 18.7 ms; ~696 MB 574 ms vs 1.50 s vs 1.25 s; ~3.2 GB no-quotes 603 ms vs 1.32 s vs 1.65 s (Rust simd-csv 870 ms); ~9.9 GB quoted 7.73 s vs 12.7 s vs 12.1 s. On all 10 files csv-zero is the fastest of the 5 parsers; ratios against zsv are 1.36x to 2.61x and against lazycsv 1.08x to 2.85x (derived from page data). csv-zero finishes the four real-world files in 0.78 to 2.86 ms (775 us on nfl.csv vs zsv 1.78 ms), so those rows include process start-up. Independent corroboration: in LangArena CSV::Parse (2026-10-05) the Zig row, which imports csv-zero, takes 0.974 s vs 2.223 s for the best C row (C/Clang) and 2.348 s for C++/Clang++.
compiler_and_flags: csv-race Makefile: Zig 'zig build --release=fast' (README names Zig 0.15.2); zsv 'cc -O3 main.c -lzsv' (libzsv's own build flags not stated); lazycsv 'g++ -std=c++17 -O3 -march=native'; Rust 'cargo build --release'. Timed with poop (perf counters) or hyperfine.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5 PRO 5650U, 30 GB RAM, Linux 6.17.8-arch1-1 (csv-race README)
why_faster: README of csv-zero: SIMD-accelerated scanning, a zero-allocation field iterator that returns slices into one internal buffer, and strict RFC 4180 validation that simplifies fast paths. The author's blog post with details (peymanmo.com) was not opened (host blocked).
stars_or_usage: 38 stars (csv-zero); companion harness csv-race has 2 stars
tradeoffs: Low-level API: yields fields (with a last-column flag), not records, and allocates nothing; strict RFC 4180 (an unquoted field containing a double quote is an error); no type conversion; Zig 0.15 to 0.17 toolchain churn; a C API exists per the README.
caveats: The harness is written by the csv-zero author and the task only counts fields, so it isolates scanning and says nothing about downstream parsing. The result chart set shows the top five parsers only; result-all.csv holds all five measured here (other csv-race parsers such as csv-parser, rapidcsv and a Go parser are in the Makefile but not in the CSV). The 'zsc (c)' label is the zsv library built via src/c/zsv, whose own compiler flags are not stated, and is linked with -lzsv (static or shared not stated), so tiny-file rows partly measure process start-up cost. Single machine (laptop-class Ryzen 5 PRO 5650U), one table. The csv-zero README claims it outperforms every library in csv-race without numbers; the numbers come from result-all.csv. zsv (C) is already catalogued as a separate entry; this record is about the Zig library.
found_via: kostya/LangArena zig/build.zig.zon dependency (peymanmortazavi/csv-zero); csv-zero README links the csv-race benchmark repository; result-all.csv read from raw.githubusercontent.com

name: cw (Rust wc clone)
baseline: BSD wc (FreeBSD 12 base system) and GNU coreutils 8.30 wc ('gwc'), both C
workload: wc-style counting of lines, words, bytes, UTF-8 characters and maximum line length on a 341,152,640-byte XML file (Dickens_Charles_Pickwick_Papers.xml, size from the README's sample output), a test-utf-8.html file, and a multi-file list run through xargs.
claimed_speedup: README hyperfine-style ratios (cw faster by) vs BSD wc / GNU wc: -l 3.44x / 4.17x; default counts 1.45x / 2.05x; -lL 1.73x / 15.07x; -m 70.36x / 30.21x (test-utf-8.html: 84.74x / 124.21x); -mlL 9.05x / 3.88x; -mLlw 3.15x / 1.35x; multi-file xargs run with --threads=12: 11.55x vs wc and 17.31x vs gwc, and 7.07x vs single-threaded cw, so single-threaded cw is about 1.6x faster than wc and 2.4x faster than gwc on that run (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: README: 'cargo build --release --features runtime-dispatch-simd' for best results (SIMD line and character counting); rustc version not stated; build flags of the FreeBSD wc and of gwc 8.30 not stated.
hardware: FreeBSD 12 on a 2.1 GHz Westmere Xeon (README)
why_faster: README: line counts use the bytecount crate, line-length counts use the memchr crate, the -m fast path counts UTF-8 characters with bytecount, and multi-file input can be counted on several threads; without -m cw works on bytes and ignores the locale.
tradeoffs: Different semantics from POSIX wc: byte counting only unless -m, no locale support, limited multibyte handling (the README lists 'improve multibyte support' and 'possibly implement locale' as future work); no test suite at the time of the README; unmaintained since 2021.
caveats: First-party numbers from one FreeBSD 12 machine in 2020-2021 against GNU coreutils 8.30. The README itself says gwc is pessimised on FreeBSD by the system's weak memchr, so Linux/glibc ratios will be smaller; newer GNU wc releases were not tested. The 70x and 124x -m ratios compare against a locale-aware multibyte path that cw does not implement for general counting. Input files other than the Dickens XML are not included, and the benchmark commands are shown only as hyperfine output. Several rows depend on multi-threading or the optional SIMD feature.
found_via: WebSearch 'implementation of wc faster than GNU wc benchmark github Haskell OR Rust ...' led to Freaky/cw; README read from raw.githubusercontent.com

name: hwc (Haskell wc)
workload: wc-style counting of bytes, words, lines, UTF-8 characters and maximum line length; only the requested statistics are computed.
claimed_speedup: README: 'about 4-6 times faster than GNU coreutils' wc, depending on the exact subset of statistics being computed' (single-threaded Haskell vs single-threaded C). No per-run timings in the repository README.
compiler_and_flags: package.yaml ghc-options: -fllvm -O2 -Wall (GHC and LLVM versions not stated); GNU wc version and flags not stated.
why_faster: README: statistics are computed in a composable, efficient manner so that only the ones the user requests are calculated; the implementation write-up (0xd34df00d.me blog post, derived from Chris Penner's wc post) was not opened (host blocked).
tradeoffs: Depends on the GHC LLVM backend and bytestring-mmap; abandoned since 2020; counts UTF-8 characters only.
caveats: Numbers are a single sentence in the README with no hardware, file size, GNU wc version, locale or timing method, so this is a first-party claim without methodology. The 4-6x range comes from the author's 2020 machine; newer GNU wc releases were not compared. Kept as a language-flavoured example (Haskell beating C wc) rather than strong evidence.

name: tuc (Rust cut replacement)
baseline: the system cut binary (C; GNU or BSD and version not stated), also awk, uutils cut, hck and choose in the same table
workload: Select fields 1, 8 and 19 (sequential and non-sequential order) from the first 1,000,000 lines of the UCI HEPMASS all_train.csv with a single-character delimiter, and from a multi-character-delimiter text file (data-multichar.txt), output to /dev/null (benchmark.sh, hyperfine --warmup 3 -m 5).
claimed_speedup: README table means: tuc -d , -f 1,8,19 1.080 s vs system cut 5.726 s (5.30x), uutils cut 1.764 s, hck 1.276 s, choose 4.347 s, awk 35.852 s (33.2x); non-sequential fields 1.093 s vs cut 5.723 s (non-sequential order); multi-character delimiter ('   '): tuc 1.464 s vs awk -F'   ' 14.471 s (9.88x) and 'tr -s | cut' 5.310 s (3.63x). With a regex delimiter (-e'\s+') tuc takes 9.870 s, no faster than hck (9.834 s).
compiler_and_flags: benchmark.sh runs 'cargo build --release'; Cargo.toml release profile lto = true, codegen-units = 1, panic = 'abort'; rustc version not stated; cut is whatever the system provides (not stated).
why_faster: The README does not state a mechanism. Visible in the table and Cargo.toml: memory-mapped input (the --no-mmap rows are about 1.14x slower) and the memchr and bstr crates (agent observation, not a source statement).
stars_or_usage: 821 stars; packaged in several distributions (repology badge)
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0-or-later (copyleft); not a drop-in cut (own CLI with ranges, negative indices, regex delimiters, JSON output); mmap input has the usual caveats on files that change while read.
caveats: First-party table; the hardware, rustc version and the cut implementation and version are not stated, and only the first 1,000,000 lines of the dataset are used. cut cannot split on a multi-character delimiter, so that table uses 'tr -s | cut' pipelines. hck is the closest competitor (1.18x slower) and is catalogued separately. Output goes to /dev/null, so write costs are excluded. Means from 5+ runs per command.

name: regex (Rust regex crate) in mariomka/regex-benchmark
baseline: PCRE2 10.36 (C, pcre2_compile and pcre2_match without JIT in the default source), Boost.Regex 1.65.1 and std::regex (g++ 7.5.0)
workload: Find and count non-overlapping matches of three patterns (email, URI, IPv4) over the concatenated 'Learn X in Y minutes' text, timing pattern compilation plus matching inside each program.
claimed_speedup: README default-settings table, total ms (email / URI / IP): Rust 57.63 (26.66 / 25.70 / 5.28), C++ Boost 104.23, C PCRE2 251.37 (126.10 / 112.17 / 13.10), C++ STL 1023.49: about 4.4x faster than PCRE2 and 17.8x faster than std::regex (derived from page data). Optimized-branch table: Rust 27.94, C PCRE2 87.87, C++ Boost 104.28, C++ STL 1021.10 (3.1x faster than PCRE2, derived). On the IP pattern alone PCRE2 is faster in the optimized table (4.73 ms vs Rust 5.11 ms).
compiler_and_flags: README versions: gcc/g++ 7.5.0 with PCRE2 10.36-2 and Boost 1.65.1.0; rustc 1.51.0 with regex 1.4.5. Compiler flags are not stated; the Dockerfile and Makefile were not inspected for optimisation flags.
hardware: MacBook Pro 16-inch 2019, 2.4 GHz Intel Core i9, 32 GB DDR4, macOS Big Sur 11.2.3, benchmark run in a Docker image (README)
why_faster: Not stated by the benchmark. The rebar README (opened) attributes the crate's speed on such patterns to its lazy DFA, in contrast to backtracking engines; the same README shows PCRE2 with JIT beating the crate on some patterns.
stars_or_usage: about 4.0k stars (rust-lang/regex); suite repo mariomka/regex-benchmark has 334 stars and is archived (last commit 2021-10-18, archived 2026-01-28)
tradeoffs: No backreferences or look-around in the regex crate; semantics differ per engine ('each language also has its engine', per the suite README).
caveats: The C program (c/benchmark.c, opened) compiles with pcre2_compile and calls pcre2_match with no pcre2_jit_compile, so PCRE2 runs interpreted; the rebar README (opened) lists pcre2/jit at 6.00 and the PCRE2 interpreter at 114.75 (geometric mean of speed ratios to the best engine, lower is better), so a JIT build would narrow the gap a lot (rust-lang/regex is also recorded from rebar under id paper:rust-regex-sys-papers). Numbers are from 2021 toolchains (rustc 1.51.0) in a Docker VM on macOS, one run per table, patterns and text chosen by the suite author. The suite repo is archived. Second claim for an already-recorded repository: keep as supporting evidence, tier B because the suite is independent but compiler flags are missing.

name: RE# (resharp, Rust derivative-based regex engine)
baseline: PCRE2 (C, through the Rust pcre2 crate 0.2 with jit_if_available(true) per the benchmark source); Rust regex and fancy-regex also measured
workload: find_all over a 1 MiB haystack for 19 common crates.io patterns, is_match latency on single values for 6 anchored validation patterns, plus lookaround scan and validate patterns (criterion benchmark popular-crates.rs).
claimed_speedup: README scan table, resharp vs PCRE2: faster on 13 of 19 patterns, slower on 6 (counted from the table); e.g. \d+ 1.76 GiB/s vs 358.25 MiB/s (5.03x), .* 2.27 GiB/s vs 768.24 MiB/s (3.03x), \d+\.\d+\.\d+ 4.86 GiB/s vs 395.43 MiB/s (12.59x), lookaround (?<="|')\s+(?=[^<>\s]+=) 2.55 GiB/s vs 406.05 MiB/s (6.42x), lookahead validate 21.28 ns vs 65.23 ns (3.07x). PCRE2 is faster on 6 (one more is a tie), e.g. <[^>]+> (2.61 vs 2.09 GiB/s), \$\{([^}]+)\} (10.66 vs 5.63 GiB/s) and (?is)<script[^>]*>.*?</script> (7.08 vs 0.81 GiB/s). Against the regex crate it is ahead on most scan rows but the README says it only matches regex throughput on standard patterns.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README; the criterion example is built through cargo with the pcre2-bench feature (resharp-engine/examples/popular-crates.rs); PCRE2 JIT enabled where available (source comment).
why_faster: README: a derivative-based, non-backtracking engine built for large alternations, lookarounds and boolean combinations (intersection, complement); on standard patterns it only matches the regex crate. The POPL paper (ACM DOI 10.1145/3704837, 'RE#') was not opened (host blocked).
stars_or_usage: 188 stars (Rust rewrite); the .NET version resharp-dotnet (258 stars) is already catalogued
tradeoffs: Leftmost-longest instead of leftmost-first match semantics; no capture groups or single-match find (is_match and find_all only); lazy quantifiers are parse errors; large alternations cost memory; capacity or lookahead overflow returns an error.
caveats: First-party table on a hand-picked set of 'popular crates.io patterns' (one row carries an unexplained asterisk); match semantics differ from PCRE2, so match counts are not guaranteed identical; PCRE2 version and compiler flags are not stated and PCRE2 comes through a Rust binding. The .NET sibling resharp-dotnet shows its large wins only over .NET regex, not over C engines. A peer-reviewed paper exists but was not readable here.

name: Crystal: LangArena Etc::Words
baseline: C++ splitting with std::istringstream and counting in std::unordered_map<std::string,int>, and C using strtok_r with uthash (strdup per new word); both built by g++/gcc 16.0.1 and clang 22.1.8; best C/C++ configuration is C++/G++/PGO at 1.587 s
workload: Split a large generated text of space-separated lowercase words and count word frequencies in a hash map, then report the most frequent word, the distinct count and a checksum (Etc::Words).
claimed_speedup: Crystal 0.88 s (peak RSS 8.8 MB) vs C++/G++ 1.638 s (-O2 'prod'), C++/G++ -O3 'Fast' 1.651 s, best of all C/C++ configurations 1.587 s (C++/G++/PGO) and C/Clang 1.988 s: about 1.9x, 1.9x, 1.8x and 2.3x faster (derived from page data). Zig 0.91 s, Rust 1.021 s and Go 1.129 s also beat every C/C++ row; the suite's 'Crystal/O3' variant row is much slower at 3.105 s.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++ (from c/Makefile and cpp/Makefile): headline 'prod' build is -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer; 'Fast' build is -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -funroll-loops with thin LTO; 'Unsafe' (-O3 -ffast-math, full LTO) and 'PGO' (-O2 plus profile) builds also exist. Compilers: clang 22.1.8 and g++/gcc 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk). Crystal 1.21.1: 'crystal build main.cr --release'; the suite also lists a 'Crystal/O3' variant row.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37)
why_faster: Not stated by the suite. Code reading (crystal/main.cr, cpp/src/words.cpp, c/src/words.c): the C++ baseline tokenizes with istringstream operator>> and copies each word into a std::string key of a node-based unordered_map; the C baseline strdup's every distinct word into uthash; Crystal splits on ' ' with a block and updates its built-in Hash. Agent inference: a tokenizer and container difference, not code generation.
tradeoffs: Crystal peak RSS 8.8 MB vs 5.3 MB for C and 7.8 MB for C++ in the same run.
caveats: Mostly a library and idiom comparison: a C++ baseline using string_view tokenizing and a flat hash map would likely close the gap, and the C baseline is slowed by per-word allocation. LangArena's own README calls it 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tasks between languages; it publishes one measurement per test and configuration (no variance) and compiles the C/C++ headline rows at -O2 with hardening flags (the -O3 'Fast', LTO, PGO and fast-math rows were also compared here and still lose). This agent selected the row because a non-C/C++ language beats every C and C++ configuration; most other tasks in the suite go the other way. Ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite.

name: Rust: LangArena Compress::BWTEncode
baseline: C (prefix-doubling suffix sort with two counting-sort passes per doubling step) and C++ (prefix doubling with std::sort on rank pairs); best C/C++ configuration is C/Gcc/Fast at 0.699 s
workload: Burrows-Wheeler transform (suffix-array construction by prefix doubling) of a generated input made of the string 'ABRACADABRA' repeated to the configured size (Compress::BWTEncode).
claimed_speedup: Rust 0.422 s (peak RSS 7.9 MB) vs C/Gcc 0.725 s (-O2 'prod'), C/Gcc -O3 'Fast' 0.699 s (best of all C/C++ configurations), C/Clang 0.739 s, C++/G++ 1.179 s and C++/Clang++ 1.259 s: about 1.7x faster than the best C row and 2.8x faster than C++/G++ (derived from page data). Swift 0.571 s also beats the C rows; Zig 1.006 s does not.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++ (from c/Makefile and cpp/Makefile): headline 'prod' build is -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer; 'Fast' build is -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -funroll-loops with thin LTO; 'Unsafe' (-O3 -ffast-math, full LTO) and 'PGO' (-O2 plus profile) builds also exist. Compilers: clang 22.1.8 and g++/gcc 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk). Rust 1.99.0: 'cargo build --release' (opt-level 3, no LTO, no target-cpu=native).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37)
why_faster: Not stated by the suite. Code reading (rust/src/benchmarks/compress.rs, c/src/compress.c, cpp/src/compress.cpp): all three use prefix doubling over rank pairs, but the sorting step differs: Rust calls the standard library's stable sort_by, C runs two counting-sort passes with fresh malloc/calloc buffers per step, C++ calls std::sort. Agent inference: the input is a short pattern repeated, so the suffix order is already nearly sorted after each step and an adaptive sort (Rust's stable sort) benefits; this is a data-dependent library effect, not code generation.
tradeoffs: Prefix doubling is O(n log^2 n) and not how production BWT code (libdivsufsort, SA-IS) works; those C libraries would be far faster than every row here.
caveats: The three implementations use different sort strategies, so same_algorithm is false; a periodic input is close to a best case for an adaptive sort. name: huniq (Rust uniq and sort -u replacement)
baseline: GNU sort -u (normal mode) and sort | uniq -c (count mode), C, versions not stated; awk (system awk, '!visited[$0]++'), datamash (C) and the author's own version 1 in C++ also measured
workload: Remove duplicate lines (and, with -c, count them) from the concatenated /usr/share/dict/* files fed 1, 2, 5, 10, 50 or 100 times (benchmark.sh, wall seconds and peak memory from 'time -f %e %M').
claimed_speedup: README tables, normal mode, huniq2-rust vs shell (sort -u): 1 repetition 0.26 s vs 7.30 s (28x, derived), 10 repetitions 3.40 s vs 93.75 s, 100 repetitions 43.65 s vs 1062.07 s (24x); vs awk 1.63 s, datamash 1.78 s and the C++ version 1 1.67 s at 1 repetition (6.4x faster than C++, derived). Count mode vs sort | uniq -c: 1.47 s vs 7.71 s at 1 repetition (5.2x), 90.80 s vs 933.67 s at 100 repetitions (10.3x); only 1.3x to 1.7x faster than the C++ version. README summary: 'around 30 times faster' than sort -u and 'between 5x and 10x' faster than sort | uniq -c.
compiler_and_flags: Cargo.toml release profile lto = 'fat' (rustc version and C++ version 1 flags not stated); the shell row runs 'sort -u' and 'sort | uniq -c' from the system (GNU, version and locale not stated).
why_faster: README: 'Sorting is slow'; huniq uses hash tables and hash sets instead of sorting the input. Cargo.toml dependencies ahash and bstr (agent observation).
tradeoffs: Hash-based, so memory grows with the number of distinct lines: 29.5 MB (dedup) and 132 MB (count) at every repetition level vs about 10 to 14 MB for sort-based pipelines; the README says the Rust version needs 10x to 12x the memory of sort | uniq in count mode. Output is not sorted (first-seen order in normal mode, unstable order in -c mode).
caveats: The speedup over sort comes from a different algorithm (hashing vs sorting), not from the language: the same author's C++ version 1 is 6.4x slower than the Rust rewrite on the same data. Hardware, tool versions and the sort locale are not stated (GNU sort is much slower in non-C locales, which could inflate the ratio); one run per table cell; the dictionary input is repeated, so high repetition levels measure mostly duplicate-heavy data. The 'shell' row is sort -u in normal mode and sort | uniq -c in count mode (from benchmark.sh).
